# /lens

Most engineers (and most agents) do this:

    get 5 signals -> treat all 5 as independent evidence -> add them up -> one hidden cause gets counted 5 times

That is mistaking shadows for sources. The signals you can measure are often not
the real thing. They are surface traces of a few causes you never get to see
directly. When four of your five signals are all driven by the same unseen cause,
adding them gives that cause four votes and buries the one signal that actually
carries something new.

The core move: do not score on the signals. Ask what small set of unseen causes,
if they existed, would generate exactly the pattern of agreement you observe. Infer
those causes from how the signals move together, then act on the causes, counting
each one once.

This is NOT /essence. /essence drops redundant columns to compress a table. /lens
goes the other way: it posits causes that are not in the table at all and explains
the columns as things those causes produced.

## When to use this

Trigger /lens when you hit any of:

- a scorer or ranker that sums several signals and one theme keeps dominating
- survey, rating, or review columns that all rise and fall together
- sensor or metric streams that agree far more than independent things should
- "we have many measurements but they seem to track just one or two underlying things"
- a recommendation or judgment that overweights whatever signal happens to be repeated
- you want to separate the part of each signal that is shared from the part that is unique

Do NOT use it when your signals are already known to be independent and each measures
a genuinely distinct thing, or when you only have one or two signals. /lens is for
the case where many surface measurements are echoes of a few unseen drivers. If there
is nothing hidden generating the agreement, there is nothing for /lens to recover.

## The procedure

1. PUT THE SIGNALS ON A COMMON FOOTING.
   Center and scale every signal so none dominates by sheer magnitude. You care how
   each signal varies, not its raw units. A loud signal must not impersonate a cause.

2. LOOK AT HOW THE SIGNALS MOVE TOGETHER.
   For every pair of signals, check whether they rise and fall as one. Signals that
   agree far more than chance allows are pointing at a shared cause behind them. This
   agreement is the only evidence you have - the cause itself is never measured.

3. POSIT A SMALL SET OF UNSEEN CAUSES.
   Hypothesize that a few hidden things generate the signals. Start with one. Each
   cause is a number per item (its strength for that item) plus a set of weights
   saying how strongly each signal reflects it.

4. GUESS THE CAUSE, THEN GUESS THE WEIGHTS, AND REPEAT.
   You know neither. So alternate. Given current weights, the best strength of the
   cause for an item is the weighted blend of that item's signals - signals that
   reflect the cause strongly count more. Given the strengths, the best weight for a
   signal is how strongly it tracks the cause across all items. Loop until both stop
   moving.

5. READ THE WEIGHTS TO SEE WHAT IS SHARED AND WHAT IS UNIQUE.
   Signals with a large weight are shadows of the cause. Signals with a near-zero
   weight reflect something the cause does not explain - those carry independent
   information. Keep that distinction; it is the whole payoff.

6. CHECK WHETHER ONE CAUSE IS ENOUGH.
   Subtract what the cause explains from each signal. If a lot of agreement remains
   in the leftover, posit a second cause and repeat steps 3 to 5 on what is left.
   Stop when the leftovers no longer agree - that is when the hidden causes are spent.

7. RE-SCORE ON THE CAUSES, NOT THE SHADOWS.
   Collapse each set of shadow signals into one reading of its cause and count that
   reading once. Add the genuinely independent signals on their own. The hidden cause
   now gets one vote instead of many.

8. SANITY-CHECK THE RECOVERED CAUSE.
   Confirm the inferred cause lines up with something real and that the independent
   signals were not wrongly folded in. A recovered cause you cannot name or explain
   is a warning, not a result (see Pitfalls).

## Output format

    INPUT: <N items x M signals, suspected to share hidden drivers>
    AGREEMENT: <which signals move together, how strongly>
    HIDDEN CAUSES: <how many causes were needed, e.g. 1>
    WEIGHTS: signal A loads 0.96, signal B loads 0.97, ... signal E loads 0.20
    SHARED vs UNIQUE: <which signals are shadows, which carry their own information>
    RECOVERED CAUSE: <what the inferred cause appears to be, and the evidence>
    RE-SCORED: <each item with the hidden cause counted once, not once per shadow>

## Composition (loops)

A scoring loop can call /lens before any signal-summing step:

    LOOP: new batch of items to rank
      on arrival -> /lens (infer hidden causes behind the signals)
                 -> /score (rank on causes, each counted once)
                 -> /verify

/lens produces the inferred causes and the shared-vs-unique split; the downstream
scorer ranks on them. /lens never makes the final ranking alone inside a loop. It
hands the de-duplicated structure to the next step so the inference stays auditable
and you can see which signals were treated as echoes of what.

## Pitfalls

- Reading a cause into pure noise. If the signals do not actually agree, the loop will
  still hand you "a cause," but it will be meaningless. Check that the agreement was
  real before you trust the recovered cause.
- Forcing one cause when there are two. If leftovers still agree after you subtract the
  first cause, you stopped too early and are blending two distinct drivers into one.
- Folding an independent signal into the shared reading. A signal with a small weight is
  carrying its own information; collapsing it into the cause throws away the one honest,
  non-redundant measurement you had.
- Skipping the common footing. If you do not center and scale first, the signal with the
  biggest raw numbers will masquerade as the hidden cause.
- Trusting a cause you cannot interpret. The math will always produce a cause. Whether it
  corresponds to something real in the world is a judgment you still have to make.

See references/logic.md for why agreement among signals lets you reconstruct a cause you never measured.
